proof:
Every point of $C$ is a convex combination of original fiber points. Grouping the combination by base and using the anchored inclusions gives $C_z=K_z$ at each $z\in P$. The affine gap $\ell_i(u,z)-u\cdot x$ is nonnegative on each generating fiber and hence throughout $C$. This gives $C_0=C$. Each cut defines a closed convex subset of $C$. Nonnegativity of the fields gives nesting.

Fix the centers $o_z$ and choose $r_z>0$ such that $o_z+r_z B_d\subseteq K_z$, where $B_d$ is the closed Euclidean unit ball. Joint continuity, compactness and finiteness bound all fields on $\mathbb S^{d-1}\times C$ by a common $M$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon\ge0$ let $\tau_z=\varepsilon M/r_z<1$. The support in direction $u$ of $o_z+(1-\tau_z)(K_z-o_z)$ is at most $h_z(u)-\tau_z r_z$, so this entire homothet satisfies every cut at $z$. If $M=0$, the cuts leave $C$ unchanged. Otherwise the homothets keep every original fiber positive and give $0\le s_\varepsilon(x)\le\varepsilon M/r_z$ for every $x\in\partial K_z$. Since all sites of $P$ remain occupied, convexity gives projection $\operatorname{conv}(P)$. Lattice completeness excludes other integer fibers, and ambient convexity gives all anchored inclusions on the deformed fibers. The affine hull is $\operatorname{aff}(P)\times\mathbb R^d$ because the projection spans $\operatorname{aff}(P)$ and any one positive fiber spans the continuous directions.

Fix a regular $x\in\partial K_z$ and abbreviate its normal by $\nu$. Put $x_\varepsilon=o_z+(1-s_\varepsilon(x))(x-o_z)$. If $\ell_i(\nu,z)=h_z(\nu)$, the cut at $\nu$ gives $s_\varepsilon(x)\nu\cdot(x-o_z)\ge\varepsilon V_i(\nu,z,x_\varepsilon)$. Since $\nu\cdot(x-o_z)\ge r_z$, the lower limit of $s_\varepsilon(x)/\varepsilon$ is at least the stated ratio, also when there is no old contact and the lower bound is zero.

For the upper limit it suffices to treat a sequence with $s_\varepsilon(x)>0$ and a positive upper limit. Then $x_\varepsilon$ is interior to $K_z$. Some cut is tight there, since otherwise compactness of the index set and continuity would give a positive minimum slack and the ray could advance. Pass to a subsequence with the tight index $i$ fixed and the tight normal $u_\varepsilon\to u_*$. The equality is
$$
\bigl[\ell_i(u_\varepsilon,z)-u_\varepsilon\cdot x\bigr]
+s_\varepsilon(x)u_\varepsilon\cdot(x-o_z)
=\varepsilon V_i(u_\varepsilon,z,x_\varepsilon).
$$
The bracket is nonnegative and is $O(\varepsilon)$ by the uniform bound on the fractional radial loss. It is the sum of the two nonnegative gaps $\ell_i(u_\varepsilon,z)-h_z(u_\varepsilon)$ and $h_z(u_\varepsilon)-u_\varepsilon\cdot x$. Both vanish at the limit. Consequently $u_*=\nu$ by regularity, and $i$ is an old contact at $\nu$. Dropping the bracket, taking the limit and using the positive limiting denominator gives the upper bound $V_i(\nu,z,x)/[\nu\cdot(x-o_z)]\le v_z(x)/[\nu\cdot(x-o_z)]$. This proves convergence also at regular points with no old contact.

The boundary of a convex body has a unique outward unit normal at surface-almost every point by local Lipschitz graph charts and Rademacher's theorem. The normal is measurable there, and the finite maximum defining $v_z$ is measurable by continuity of the gaps and fields. For each old boundary point $x$, the removed radial layer consists, up to volume-null endpoints, of the points $o_z+(1-s)(x-o_z)$ for $0\le s<s_\varepsilon(x)$. The radial change of variables has Jacobian $(1-s)^{d-1}\nu_z(x)\cdot(x-o_z)$ with respect to $dS(x)\,ds$. Indeed its $d-1$ tangent derivatives have factor $1-s$, and the remaining derivative is $-(x-o_z)$. The area formula applies in the Lipschitz boundary charts, and distinct rays give distinct points in the thin layer. When $d=1$ these two layers are endpoint intervals of lengths $s_\varepsilon(x)|x-o_z|$. Dividing the layer integral by $\varepsilon$, the uniform radial bound gives domination, and the pointwise radial limit gives the integral of $v_z$.

If a fiber is wholly captured, the fixed cap takes its whole removed volume. If the cap misses the fiber interior, it takes zero removed volume. Otherwise the cap's cutting plane meets $\operatorname{int}K_z$. Its intersection with $\partial K_z$ is contained in the relative boundary of the section in that plane. Indeed a support at a relative interior point of the section would have to contain the cutting plane, which crosses the interior of the body. The relative boundary of this $(d-1)$-dimensional convex section has zero $(d-1)$-measure. For $d=1$ the section is an interior point and misses both endpoints. At all other old boundary points, a sufficiently thin removed layer has the same cap status as the point. Inserting the cap indicator in the radial integral and applying the same domination gives the selector formula. There are finitely many bases, and taking the maximum of finitely many normalized remainders gives uniformity for each fixed finite cap list.
statement:
Let $n\ge0$, $d\ge1$, and let $P=\operatorname{conv}(P)\cap\mathbb Z^n$ be finite and nonempty. For each $z\in P$ let $K_z\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a compact convex body with nonempty interior. Assume $\sum_z\lambda_z K_z\subseteq K_p$ whenever $\lambda_z\ge0$, $\sum_z\lambda_z=1$, and $\sum_z\lambda_z z=p\in P$. Put $C=\operatorname{conv}\bigcup_{z\in P}(\{z\}\times K_z)$ and $h_z=h_{K_z}$.

A finite global-cut action on $C$ uses a nonempty finite index set $I$. For each $i\in I$, its function $\ell_i(u,z)$ is continuous in $u\in\mathbb S^{d-1}$ and affine in $z\in\operatorname{aff}(P)$, with $\ell_i(u,z)\ge h_z(u)$ on $P$. Its field $V_i(u,z,x)$ is jointly continuous and nonnegative on $\mathbb S^{d-1}\times C$ and convex in $(z,x)$ on $C$ for each fixed $u$. Fields satisfying these assumptions on a larger common convex domain can be restricted to $C$. For $\varepsilon\ge0$ define
$$
C_\varepsilon=C\cap
\bigcap_{i\in I,\;u\in\mathbb S^{d-1}}
\{(z,x):u\cdot x+\varepsilon V_i(u,z,x)\le\ell_i(u,z)\}.
$$
Then $C_0=C$, and for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon\ge0$, $C_\varepsilon$ is a nested compact convex body in $\operatorname{aff}(P)\times\mathbb R^d$. Its projection is $\operatorname{conv}(P)$, its integer fibers $K_z(\varepsilon)=(C_\varepsilon)_z$ have nonempty interior exactly for $z\in P$, and it has no other integer fibers. The deformed fibers satisfy all the same anchored Minkowski inclusions.

At a regular $x\in\partial K_z$, with unique outward unit normal $\nu_z(x)$, define
$$
v_z(x)=\max\Bigl(\{V_i(\nu_z(x),z,x):i\in I,\ \ell_i(\nu_z(x),z)=h_z(\nu_z(x))\}\cup\{0\}\Bigr).
$$
About each fixed $o_z\in\operatorname{int}K_z$, let $s_\varepsilon(x)$ be the fractional radial loss, so the new endpoint on the ray through $x$ is $o_z+(1-s_\varepsilon(x))(x-o_z)$. The ratios $s_\varepsilon(x)/\varepsilon$ are uniformly bounded in $x\in\partial K_z$ and, at each regular $x$, tend to $v_z(x)/[\nu_z(x)\cdot(x-o_z)]$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Thus
$$
|K_z|-|K_z(\varepsilon)|=\varepsilon\int_{\partial K_z}v_z\,dS+o(\varepsilon),
\qquad dS=d\mathcal H^{d-1}.
$$

Let $\mu_\varepsilon(H)=\sum_{z\in P}|K_z(\varepsilon)\cap H_z|$, where $H_z=\{x:(z,x)\in H\}$ for a fixed closed ambient halfspace $H$. On $\partial K_z$, let $\kappa_{z,H}$ be $1$ if $K_z\subseteq H_z$, $0$ if $\operatorname{int}K_z\cap H_z=\varnothing$, and $\mathbf1_{\operatorname{int}H_z}$ otherwise. The first case includes an inside supporting cut and a pure-base cut whose boundary contains the whole fiber. The second includes an outside supporting trace, even when that trace has positive surface measure. Then
$$
\mu_0(H)-\mu_\varepsilon(H)=\varepsilon L(H)+o(\varepsilon),
\qquad L(H)=\sum_{z\in P}\int_{\partial K_z}\kappa_{z,H}v_z\,dS.
$$
The first total loss is $D=\sum_{z\in P}\int_{\partial K_z}v_z\,dS$. The remainders can be taken uniformly on each fixed finite cap list. For $d=1$, $dS$ is counting measure on the two endpoints.
title: Radial speed and fixed closed-cap loss for finite global cuts
